extracted.intended_audience: judges, lawyers, criminal investigators, police surgeons, and forensic examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing the reliability of witness sensory reports, hallucinations, and imaginative reconstructions in forensic and legal contexts; includes how disease, drugs, fatigue, and imagination affect testimony and how to collect/corroborate sensory evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on testimony based solely on touch
rubrics_metrics.description: But important and reliable as the sense of touch is, it is nevertheless not to be trusted when it is the sole instrument of perception. We must never depend on the testimony of a witness based entirely on perceptions by touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require corroboration (e.g., sight or other evidence) for tactile-based statements. Examples: wounded persons often misjudge time, manner, strength, and location of wounds; blows are felt as pain and misestimated; victims frequently misattribute which wound caused which sensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect wound evidence by detailed tabulation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is best done by means of tabulation, accurate description of wounds according to their place, size, form, and significance, the statement of the victim concerning his feeling at the moment of receiving the wound, the consequences of healing, and at the end explanatory observations concerning the reasons for true or incorrect sensations of the victim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record objective wound characteristics and subjective sensations separately; compare subjective feelings with objective deeds. Veracity of the victim is less relevant for psychological study of perception; the goal is to detect patterns and generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of tactile spatial and pressure illusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern psychophysics has pointed to a large group of false perceptions due to illusions of pressure, stabs, or other contact with the skin. The best known experiments are those with open compasses; pressed on less sensitive parts they are always felt as one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that touch poorly discriminates two close points and weights without visual cues (e.g., varied objects judged equal in weight). Use this knowledge when evaluating tactile testimony (back, thigh, less sensitive areas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactile localization depends on learned body maps and vision
rubrics_metrics.description: When fingers or hands are placed in unusual positions tactile localization is lost or doubled; experience and sight normally correct such anomalies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume precise localization from touch alone (e.g., crossing fingers example, crossed hands causing misidentification). Consider whether the witness had usual sensory configuration/experience at the time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for transferability and vicarious tactile sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: A sort of transferability of certain touch sensations exists: e.g., if ants are busy near my seat I immediately feel that ants are running about under my clothes, and if I see a wound or hear it described, I often feel pain in the analogous place on my own body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that contagious or suggestive sensations can lead excitable witnesses to report sensations they did not actually experience; corroboration is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider relative and contrast effects on tactile perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactile sensations are counted only relatively and their value varies with the individual (e.g., one hand in hot and one in cold water then both in tepid water produces different impressions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about absolute tactile claims; prior exposures can alter subsequent tactile judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider physiological and pharmacological effects on touch
rubrics_metrics.description: Diseased conditions and poisons affect touch: slight poisonings by chloroform, morphine, atropine, daturine, decrease, and strychnine increases the sensitivity of the touch organ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to physician when sensory sensitivity may be altered by drugs or disease; factor this into evaluation of tactile testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat gustatory (taste) testimony as especially unreliable
rubrics_metrics.description: Illusions of taste are of importance only in cases of poisoning; taste and odor are particularly difficult to get unanimity about and therefore hard to understand possible illusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because disease, prior poisoning, and imagination alter taste (e.g., rose-santonin causes persistent bitter taste; morphine causes bitter/sour; intermittent fevers cause metallic tastes), taste-based accusations (poisoning) require independent confirmation and inquiry into recent ingestion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for imagination and expectation effects on taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagination makes considerable difference; if some salt meat is taken to be a sweet pastry, the taste becomes disgusting because imaginary and actual tastes mix. The eye has especial influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always ask what had been eaten or drunk before; consider labels/expectations and visual cues as strong modulators of taste reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior tastes and preconceived notions strongly bias gustatory perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior tastes may cause significant gustatory illusions; the illusions are greatest especially when a thing has been tasted with a preconceived notion of its taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat taste testimony as reliable without corroboration; housewives' practice of sequencing food/wine illustrates practical relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat olfactory (smell) reports cautiously and seek medical input when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Olfactory illusions are very rare in healthy people and frequent among the mentally diseased; certain poisons tend to debauch the olfactory sense (strychnine makes it finer, morphine duller).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Call in a physician when olfactory hallucination is suspected; suspect disease (e.g., lung conditions) when witnesses insist on inhaling poisoned air. Recognize mental disease associations (sexual conditions, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize imagination and association heavily bias olfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Many odors are in the air and not very powerfully differentiated and may be turned by means of the imagination into that one which is most obvious; associative memories determine pleasantness/unpleasantness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements by witnesses concerning perceptions of odor are valueless unless otherwise confirmed. Consider associative histories (e.g., flowers associated with coffins) that bias odor reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish (and treat cautiously) illusions versus hallucinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Illusion implies misinterpretation of an external object; hallucination implies no external object. Limits are not definite; phenomena overlap and both may require physician involvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When faced with alleged hallucination or illusion, lawyers must call in physicians for assessment. However, avoid calling physicians for every fanciful or false statement; balance is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Many ordinary witness reports may be affected by hallucinations/illusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Hallucinations and illusions may occur in normal people under fatigue, fever, isolation, constipation, great danger, hunger, loss of blood, menstruation, or pain; even non-pathological persons can experience them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigorously test witness statements rather than assume deliberate falsehood; consider situational/physiological causes for sensory reports (e.g., seeing a thief that was hallucinated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand neurological/excitatory causes of hallucinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The cause of hallucination and illusion is sought in over-excitement of the cerebro-spinal system; stimulation intensity ranges from momentary rush of blood to complete lunacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When hallucinations are possible, medical/physiological explanation should be investigated; symptoms may range from trivial to indicators of serious mental disturbance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate imaginative ideas from passive hallucinations/illusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Illusions and hallucinations differ from imaginative representations because the latter are more active; imaginative combinations are produced by the individual rather than passively received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a contested report results from active imagination (creative recombination) or passive perception; this affects how to test and corroborate the statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: To evaluate imaginative-origin statements, decompose and reconstruct elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever we believe a statement to be based on imagination, we must always connect it with its most proximate neighbors, and step by step seek out its elements and then compound them in the simplest possible form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive a plausible starting-point from the imaginative report, reconstruct the simplest compound from elements, and compare it to all available material — only if they agree may the starting-point be considered proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be attentive to imagination-induced psychosomatic phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagination can produce bodily symptoms: e.g., B feels a blow and then develops unconsciousness and signs of brain injury because he imagined being struck with the ball.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that subjective physical symptoms can be induced by imagination without external cause; investigate objectively rather than assume external trauma automatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for social reinforcement and collective acceptance of improbable scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: When others help us and perform improbable acts (e.g., opera conventions), we accept improbable constructions as possible and affective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider communal or performative reinforcement when evaluating witness testimony that may be socially amplified or ritualized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize individual differences in imaginative content and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Each person imagines differently according to character, experience, and habitual imagery; what one perceives in clouds or a work of art varies widely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming a universal meaning for symbolic or imaginative reports; consider the witness's background, imagination strength, and tendencies when interpreting their statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small, mild impressions may stimulate imagination more than strong ones
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of imagination is much more stimulated by mild, peaceful impressions than by vigorous ones; small impressions pass unnoticed until they find congenial soil and ferment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to subtle cues that could have triggered imaginative reconstructions; these are harder to detect and may be easily missed in testimony analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral signs are unreliable indicators of imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: We rarely can tell whether a man's imagination is at work; external indices (like quiet hands/feet for anger) are imperfect and do not reliably indicate imaginative activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not over-interpret behavioral cues as definitive evidence of imagination or its absence; corroborate with other evidence and context.
